1: # opencode-readonly-guard
2: 
3: Make opencode's read-only agents (`plan`, `explore`, and any agent with `edit: deny`) actually read-only.
4: 
5: In opencode, "plan mode" is a request to the model, not a restriction: the `plan` and `explore` agents can run any
6: shell command, so a model that ignores the reminder can still `rm`, `sed -i` or `> file`. This plugin closes that gap:
7: 
8: - **Write guard.** Before opencode evaluates any permission rule, the full command line is parsed and refused if it
9:   writes: redirections in any position, `tee` to a file, `rm`/`cp`/`mv`/…, `sed -i`, `git commit`, `npm install`,
10:   `find -delete`, `curl -o`, and wrappers around them (`sudo`, `env`, `xargs`, `bash -c`, `$(…)`). The model gets an
11:   error that tells it to return the data in its reply instead.
12: - **Shared allowlist.** Read-only agents ask before running anything except a vetted list of read-only commands
13:   (`ls`, `cat`, `rg`, `git log`, `herdr agent list`, …). The list lives in [`rules/`](rules) as plain JSON that anyone
14:   can extend.
15: - **Reviewed learning.** An "always" answer in a read-only agent is only logged as a candidate. `/guard-review` shows
16:   candidates with safe pattern options, and a rule is added only after you confirm the exact pattern.
17: - **Event log.** Every shell command, block, prompt and answer in a read-only agent is recorded, so the policy can be
18:   improved with data.
19: 
20: Tested with opencode 1.19.3 (supported range `>=1.18.29 <2`). opencode 2.x has a different plugin API and is not
21: supported yet, see [TODO.md](TODO.md).
22: 
23: ## Install
24: 
25: ```sh
26: opencode plugin opencode-readonly-guard --global   # adds it to ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json
27: ```
28: 
29: or add it to your config by hand, with options if you want them:
30: 
31: ```jsonc
32: // opencode.json
33: {
34:   "plugin": [
35:     "opencode-readonly-guard",
36:     // or: ["opencode-readonly-guard", { "agents": { "include": ["reviewer"] }, "allow": ["whoami *"] }]
37:   ],
38: }
39: ```
40: 
41: Restart opencode afterwards (config and plugins are loaded once at startup).
42: 
43: Other ways:
44: 
45: | Tool        | Command                                                                           |
46: | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
47: | npm / bun   | `npm i -g opencode-readonly-guard` · `bun add -g opencode-readonly-guard`         |
48: | mise (CLI)  | `mise use -g npm:opencode-readonly-guard`                                         |
49: | From source | `git clone … && mise run setup build`, then `"plugin": ["file:///path/to/clone"]` |
50: 
51: > The package is not published to npm yet (see [TODO.md](TODO.md)). Until then, use the from-source route.
52: 
53: Load it once (not from both a global and a project config): two copies would both inject rules, register the same
54: tools and log every event twice.
55: 
56: ## Using it
57: 
58: **`/guard-review`** (registered by the plugin, runs in `build`) summarizes the log: blocked commands, the most-prompted
59: commands and allowlist candidates. For each candidate you pick the exact rule to keep (the exact command, the same
60: command limited to its directory, or opencode's general pattern, whichever the safety check accepts) or dismiss it.
61: opencode then asks you to confirm that exact pattern before it is written to `readonly-guard.json`. New rules apply
62: after a restart. In read-only agents the review tools are hidden, so an agent cannot extend its own allowlist.
63: 
64: **Command-line tool** (`opencode-readonly-guard`, also available as `npx opencode-readonly-guard`):
65: 
66: ```text
67: check [--json] [--no-store] <command>   what a read-only agent gets: allow | ask | block (exit status 0 | 1 | 2)
68: vet <pattern>                           may this pattern be added to the allowlist?
69: rules [--json]                          print the shared allowlist and the always-ask flags
70: review [--limit N]                      print the log summary
71: install [-g] [--force]                  opencode plugin opencode-readonly-guard
72: ```
73: 
74: ```console
75: $ opencode-readonly-guard check 'git log --oneline | head'
76: allow
77: $ opencode-readonly-guard check 'ls | cat > notes.txt'
78: block  write redirection "> notes.txt"
79: $ opencode-readonly-guard check 'whoami'
80: ask    needs approval: whoami
81: ```
82: 
83: ## How the policy is built
84: 
85: For every read-only agent the plugin writes this ordered bash rule list into the config (the last matching rule wins):
86: 
87: 1. `"*": ask`
88: 2. the shared allowlist, [`rules/allow.json`](rules/allow.json)
89: 3. presets that are on (see [Working inside herdr](#working-inside-herdr)), learned rules (`readonly-guard.json`) and
90:    the `allow` option, each re-checked at startup
91: 4. the agent's own bash rules, if it had any
92: 5. the always-ask flags, [`rules/ask.json`](rules/ask.json): `find -delete/-exec`, `rg --pre`, `git … --output`, …
93: 
94: Because the flags come last, a broad learned rule such as `find *` never silences `find . -delete`.
95: 
96: Read-only agents are `plan`, `explore`, every agent whose `permission.edit` is `deny` (or `tools.edit: false`), plus
97: `agents.include`, minus `agents.exclude`. `plan` additionally asks before delegating to a subagent that is not
98: read-only, and never to `general`.
99: 
100: ## Working inside herdr
101: 
102: Agents that run in a [herdr](https://herdr.dev) pane can inspect it with the `herdr` CLI. The rules treat `herdr` like
103: `git`: they judge the subcommand, never the program as a whole (`herdr *` is never accepted).
104: 
105: - **Allowed without a prompt:** `--help`, `--version`, `--skill`, a bare command group (`herdr agent`, `herdr pane`, …)
106:   and the read-only subcommands: `status`, `agent list|get|read|wait|explain`,
107:   `pane list|current|get|layout|process-info|neighbor|edges|read|wait-output`, `workspace|tab list|get`,
108:   `worktree|session|machine|plugin|integration` listings, `api snapshot|schema`, `config check`, `channel show`.
109: - **Always asks**, even when an agent's own rules allow `herdr *`, and can never be learned (exact or with a wildcard):
110:   every other subcommand, such as `pane send-text|send-keys|run|split|close`, `agent prompt|send-keys|start`,
111:   `tab|workspace create|close|focus`, `server stop`, `session stop`. A read-only agent must not send instructions to
112:   another agent, so `agent prompt` stays a prompt. The `--machine`, `--session` and `--remote` prefixes, bare `herdr`
113:   (it opens the terminal UI) and `--trust-repository` ask too.
114: - **Blocked** like other writes: `herdr update`, `worktree create|remove`, `config reset-keys`,
115:   `integration install|uninstall`, `session delete`, `plugin install|update`, `api schema --output FILE`, and
116:   `pane run PANE CMD` when `CMD` would itself be blocked (`herdr pane run w1:p2 'rm -rf build'`).
117: - **UI commands, on inside herdr:** `herdr tab rename` and `herdr notification show` only change what herdr
118:   displays, which is how a plan-mode agent can report its state. They are the `herdr-ui` preset: allowed without a
119:   prompt when opencode runs in a herdr pane (`HERDR_ENV=1`), and not otherwise. Outside a pane the herdr CLI still
120:   reaches the running session and acts on whatever is focused there, so a UI command listed in your store or options
121:   is ignored outside herdr too. The preset is built into the plugin and is not part of the shared allowlist.
122: 
123:   Switch it off with `"presets": { "herdr-ui": false }`, and list the one command you want instead:
124: 
125:   ```jsonc
126:   // ~/.config/opencode/readonly-guard.json (the store), or in the plugin options,
127:   // or in herdr's own directory: ~/.config/herdr/readonly-guard.json
128:   { "presets": { "herdr-ui": false }, "allow": ["herdr tab rename *"] }
129:   ```
130: 
131:   Where the settings come from:
132: 
133:   | Source                                  | Keys                    | Notes                                                       |
134:   | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
135:   | plugin options in `opencode.json`       | `presets`, `allow`      | lowest precedence                                           |
136:   | the store `readonly-guard.json`         | `presets`, `allow`, ... | the file `/guard-review` writes                             |
137:   | `readonly-guard.json` in herdr's config | `presets`, `allow`      | read only inside herdr, never written, wins over the others |
138: 
139:   herdr's directory is the one holding `$HERDR_CONFIG_PATH`, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/herdr` (`~/.config/herdr`). If
140:   sources disagree about a preset, the last in the table wins; `allow` lists add up. Every `allow` pattern passes the
141:   same safety check, so no file can allow `herdr agent prompt`, and herdr's file may only hold `herdr …` patterns.
142:   `opencode-readonly-guard vet 'herdr tab rename *'` shows what the safety check says about a pattern, and `check`
143:   follows the same rules as the plugin (`--no-store` means the shared rules only: no store, no presets).
144: 
145: herdr is not in opencode's table of known programs, so an "always" answer to any herdr prompt is saved by opencode as
146: `herdr *`, for every agent until restart. The write guard still blocks the commands above, but nothing stops
147: `herdr pane send-text`. Answer "once" to herdr prompts. rtk does not rewrite herdr commands, so there are no `rtk herdr`
148: rules.
149: 
150: ## Options
151: 
152: Set them with the tuple form: `["opencode-readonly-guard", { … }]`.
153: 
154: | Option           | Default                                         | Meaning                                                         |
155: | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
156: | `agents.include` | `[]`                                            | extra agents to treat as read-only (they must exist)            |
157: | `agents.exclude` | `[]`                                            | agents to leave alone                                           |
158: | `allow`          | `[]`                                            | extra bash patterns to allow; each passes the same safety check |
159: | `presets`        | `{}`                                            | switch built-in rule sets on or off: `{ "herdr-ui": false }`    |
160: | `store`          | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode/readonly-guard.json` | learned rules, dismissed candidates, agent lists                |
161: | `logDir`         | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/readonly-guard`        | `events.jsonl` (rotated at 5 MB to `events.old.jsonl`)          |
162: | `toast`          | `true`                                          | warn when an "always" answer is given in a read-only agent      |
163: | `command`        | `"guard-review"`                                | name of the review command, or `false` to not register it       |
164: 
165: `READONLY_GUARD_STORE` and `READONLY_GUARD_DATA` override the default paths (an explicit option wins). The store file
166: is plain JSON and safe to keep in your dotfiles; the event log contains the commands your agents ran, so keep it local.
167: The startup `init` event in the log lists the `presets` in effect next to the number of `learned` rules.
168: 
169: ## What it does not do
170: 
171: This is an accident preventer and a policy engine, not a sandbox.
172: 
173: - Only the `bash`/`shell` tool is covered. MCP tools, `webfetch` and others follow opencode's normal permissions.
174: - Interpreters can write (`python -c`, `node -e`, `awk`, `sqlite3 .shell`). They are not on the allowlist, so they
175:   prompt, but the guard does not read their code, and a broad "always" answer would let them through.
176: - Parsing is a hand-written approximation of POSIX shell; anything it cannot parse is blocked rather than guessed.
177: - Linux and macOS shells only. PowerShell is not parsed.
178: - "Always" answers made in opencode itself stay in effect for all agents until restart, see the findings below. The
179:   plugin warns, logs them and keeps the write guard on top, but it cannot revoke them.
180: 
181: ## Findings about opencode 1.19.3
182: 
183: What building this taught us. Each point was checked against the binary or by a live run, and several are worth an
184: upstream issue (they are in [TODO.md](TODO.md)).
185: 
186: **Permissions**
187: 
188: - Plan mode is a prompt. The `plan` agent only denies the `edit` tool (except plan files); its `bash` is `* allow`
189:   and so is `explore`'s. The "READ-ONLY phase" text is a reminder injected into the conversation.
190: - Rules are evaluated in order and the last match wins; `*` matches anything and a trailing ` *` also matches the bare
191:   command.
192: - Bash commands are split with tree-sitter and each simple command is matched on its own text. That text includes a
193:   redirection only when the command's direct parent is the redirection, so `cat a > b` is matched as written, while
194:   the redirections of later pipeline stages (`a | b > f`), `{ …; } > f` and `( … ) > f` are invisible to patterns.
195:   Glob rules therefore cannot stop those writes; a parser in `tool.execute.before` can.
196: - Commands inside `$(…)`, backticks and `<(…)` are checked as separate commands.
197: 
198: **"Always" answers**
199: 
200: - The saved pattern is the command prefix plus `*`, using a built-in table of how many words matter (`git log *`,
201:   `npm view *`) and falling back to the first word. Unknown programs become `prog *`: answering "always" to
202:   `tee /dev/null` allowed `tee *`, and for anything rewritten by the rtk plugin it is `rtk *`.
203: - It is kept in memory for the whole opencode process, is checked after every agent's rules (so it beats `ask` and
204:   `deny`), applies to all agents and sessions, and is lost on restart. The `permission` table in the database stays
205:   empty.
206: 
207: **Plugin API**
208: 
209: - `tool.execute.before` runs before the permission check; throwing from it aborts the tool call and the message reaches
210:   the model. This is what makes the write guard possible.
211: - The `permission.ask` hook is declared in the types and docs but is never called. A plugin cannot answer prompts
212:   itself, so learning has to go through a review step.
213: - The `config` hook may edit `agent.<name>.permission`; the rules end up after the built-in ones in the resolved
214:   agent (`opencode debug agent <name>` shows them). A permission set globally is appended after every agent's rules.
215: - `chat.params` reports the agent of each model call, including subagents. The utility agents `title`, `summary` and
216:   `compaction` share the session, so they must be ignored when tracking which agent a session belongs to. The v1 SDK
217:   types do not expose `agent` on sessions, but the runtime does (used as a fallback).
218: - Permission events are `permission.asked` / `permission.replied` at runtime, although the v1 SDK types still say
219:   `permission.updated`.
220: - Plugin tools can call `context.ask()` to raise a permission prompt. Agents start from `* allow`, so the plugin adds a
221:   global `readonly_guard_allow: ask` rule (evaluated after every agent's rules) to force the confirmation prompt.
222: 
223: **Plugin packaging (v1)**
224: 
225: - opencode treats every export of a plugin module as a plugin and calls it. Export only the default definition.
226: - A package is loaded from `exports["./server"]`, else `main`. A default export `{ id, server }` is supported since
227:   1.18.29. `engines.opencode` is enforced. Peer dependencies such as `@opencode-ai/plugin` are installed for you.
228: - opencode 2.x plugins are `Plugin.define({ id, setup })`, V1 plugins do not run there, and V2 has a real
229:   `permission.hook("evaluate")` that would remove most of these workarounds.
230: 
231: **Models and tooling**
232: 
233: - Models in plan mode often refuse to run a write command to "test" the guard, because of the reminder. To exercise
234:   it, delegate to `explore` from `build`, or use an `edit: deny` harness agent (see the e2e tests).
235: - The rtk plugin rewrites commands (`ls` → `rtk ls`) before permissions are evaluated, so patterns must match the
236:   rewritten form (the allowlist has `rtk …` entries). Models then see a command they did not write and retry it
237:   several times, which wastes tokens (observed with Haiku and Sonnet).
238: - When spawning `opencode run` from another program, set `PWD` to the working directory (opencode trusts it over the
239:   real cwd; a mismatch fails with an `UnknownError`).
240: 
241: ## Development
242: 
243: Everything is managed with [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev); Git hooks with [hk](https://hk.jdx.dev).
244: 
245: ```sh
246: mise install                # bun, node, hk, actionlint, shellcheck and the pinned opencode
247: mise run setup              # bun install + git hooks (prettier, oxlint, tsc, conventional commits)
248: mise run check              # lint, formatting, types, unit tests (what CI runs)
249: mise run test:integration   # builds, then drives the real opencode without a model, and a packed tarball
250: mise run test:e2e           # opt-in, real model: E2E_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5
251: mise tasks                  # all tasks
252: ```
253: 
254: Code style follows opencode: TypeScript (strict, NodeNext), no semicolons, 120 columns, oxlint, prettier. See
255: [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for adding rules and test cases.
256: 
257: ## License
258: 
259: [MIT](LICENSE), the same as opencode.

(End of file - total 259 lines)
</content>

**Input:**
```json

  "command": "herdr --skill 2>&1 | head -150"

```

**Output:**
```
---
name: herdr
description: "Control Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Use only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr or asks to use Herdr to inspect or control panes, tabs, workspaces, commands, or another agent. Do not use merely because a task could benefit from a background terminal, delegation, or parallel work. Requires HERDR_ENV=1."
---

# Herdr

Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.

Before issuing any control command, verify that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:

```bash
test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
```

If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.

When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the current session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create terminal layout, start agents and commands, read output, and wait for state changes.

## Learn the current CLI

The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Start with:

```bash
herdr --help
```

Then print the relevant command group by running the group without a subcommand:

```bash
herdr agent
herdr pane
herdr workspace
herdr tab
herdr worktree
herdr terminal
herdr notification
herdr integration
herdr session
herdr machine
```

Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments. Commands such as `herdr workspace create` are valid with defaults and will execute.

Most control commands return JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting them.

## Understand layout, panes, and agents

Choose the primitive that matches the job:

- Workspace, tab, and pane topology organize terminal locations.
- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.

A pane exists whether or not it contains an agent. `agent start` requires an existing available shell pane and never creates, splits, or moves layout. Use pane commands for ordinary processes. Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.

Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced. Suspending an agent with Ctrl+Z and running a non-agent command preserves its identity while the exact process remains alive. This does not preserve the original identity across another recognized agent taking over. A retained identity does not mean the agent is in the foreground; inspect the pane before sending input.

`idle` and `done` normally indicate the agent is ready for input; neither guarantees that an unfamiliar approval dialog was recognized or that a retained agent is in the foreground. The CLI/API uses the server's seen state to distinguish them; explicit focus commands mark the target seen, while reads do not. Each TUI client tracks viewed completions independently, so its Done badge can differ from the CLI or another client's badge. Antigravity and Grok can be idle while background tasks or subagents keep running, so a settled-state wait is not proof those jobs have finished. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.

## Use IDs and caller context

Public IDs are opaque stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`

Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new workspace-qualified pane ID. After `pane move`, continue with `.result.move_result.pane.pane_id` or the live agent name. The old value is reported as `.result.move_result.previous_pane_id`; only the moved process's inherited caller context keeps resolving that old ID, so do not use it as a general agent target.

Herdr injects the caller's context into each managed pane:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. An omitted `pane split` target uses the calling pane when `HERDR_PANE_ID` is available, otherwise the focused pane. Other commands may use the UI-focused pane, which can belong to the user or another client.

Discover live state with:

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr pane current --current
herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr agent list
```

Creation responses expose the IDs to use next. `workspace create` returns `.result.workspace`, `.result.tab`, and `.result.root_pane`. `tab create` returns `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`. `pane split` returns the new pane as `.result.pane`.

IDs and live agent names are scoped to one server. Two saved SSH machines can both have `w1:p1` or an agent named `reviewer`. Selecting a machine in the TUI does not retarget commands running in your pane: without `--machine`, they still use the inherited session and socket context.

To control a saved SSH machine, use the same global prefix for discovery and every later command:

```bash
herdr --machine <label-or-id> agent list
herdr --machine <label-or-id> pane list
herdr --machine <label-or-id> agent prompt <remote-agent-name> "Reply with your current status." --wait --timeout 120000
```

The selector must be an enabled saved profile ID or a unique, case-sensitive label, not an arbitrary SSH hostname. Commands use that profile's remote session without an open TUI. Do not combine `--machine` with `--session` or `--remote`. Discover IDs on that machine; inherited local IDs and `--current` do not identify remote panes.

Both installations must support machine API forwarding, and the remote server must already be running and API-compatible. Forwarding never installs, starts, or restarts a server and never falls back to Local. Local configuration, session management, installation commands, and interactive attachment are not forwarded. Remote worktree paths must be absolute, `~`, or start with `~/`; plugin link paths must be absolute. A connection failure does not prove a mutation was not applied: inspect remote state before retrying.

`herdr machine list` lists saved connection profiles, not a cross-machine pane inventory; add `--json` for scripts. Only add, remove, enable, or disable profiles when the user asks. Removing a profile disconnects the client but does not stop remote sessions. Interactive `machine add` discovers running remote sessions and may ask the user to pick one; non-interactive setup uses the remote default session unless `--remote-session` is explicitly supplied. Use `herdr machine status [<label-or-id>] --json` to diagnose a failing machine. `herdr machine reconnect` needs the user to complete SSH authentication in their terminal; do not run it for them. Setup asks before stopping an incompatible server and defaults to No; do not approve replacement without the user's consent. Experimental handoff is not part of `machine add`.

## Start and coordinate an agent

Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and the current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.

Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane:

```bash
herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane and explicitly preserve the caller's working directory:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Replace `right` with `down` when appropriate. Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`.

An available shell pane must be at its interactive prompt, with the shell itself in the foreground and no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Start a supported agent in that pane with a useful unique name:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id>
```

Use the kind requested by the user. Run `herdr agent` to inspect the installed kind list and options. Pass native agent arguments only after `--`:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id> -- <agent-args...>
```

A successful `agent start` returns only after Herdr detects the expected agent in the same pane and considers it ready for interactive input. If the agent is blocked during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately but keeps the name available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`. Wait until the agent becomes idle before prompting it. Startup defaults to a 30-second timeout.

Submit work through the agent surface:

```bash
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings." --wait --timeout 120000
```

`agent prompt` honors the pane's live bracketed-paste mode and sends text followed by encoded Enter as one ordered submission. It reports successful submission only after both have been written; that alone does not prove the agent started a turn. For Codex on Windows, Herdr sends a paste boundary before Enter so submission does not depend on prompt size. It rejects an agent already waiting at an approval or question dialog with `agent_blocked` before sending any input. Inspect the blocked UI and ask the user before answering it. For normal agent work, `--wait` is enough: it waits for the first settled `idle`, `done`, or `blocked` state. Do not repeat those defaults with `--until`.

With `--wait`, a prompt sent from a non-working state must produce observed `working` or `blocked` activity. After submission, Herdr waits up to five seconds for that activity; unrelated `idle`, `done`, or session changes do not satisfy this gate. It returns `agent_prompt_stalled` if no activity is observed, or `timeout` if the caller's timeout expires first. The caller timeout includes submission time. Without a timeout, the settled-state wait is indefinite after activity is observed. This wait tracks lifecycle state, not an individual turn; if the agent is already working, completion of the active turn may satisfy it.

Use `--until` only for a state-specific workflow, such as waiting for an already-running agent to request input:


```

## Assistant (Plan · Claude Opus 5.5 · 8.1s)

_Thinking:_
This review output points to a likely bug: commands like `echo ---` show up as pipeline stages the user approved with "always," and opencode seems to save patterns broadly across the whole pipeline rather than per-command. I'm also noticing several commands that should probably be allowlisted already but aren't, like `echo`, `sort`, and `tr`.

Given the scale of this data (818 events), I don't want to manually trace through everything — that's a job for a worker, not something to burn context on directly. For now, in plan mode, I just want enough aggregate signal to scope step 1 properly, so I'll check allow.json's contents and pull together quick stats on the most-prompted and most-blocked commands.

I realize `asked.patterns` actually captures every stage of the compound command, not just the ones that triggered the prompt — so the review's candidate counts are inflated by already-allowed stages like echo and head, making "echo ---" look like the top trigger when it was really npm view. This looks like a data-quality issue in the review tool itself, and to pinpoint the actual triggering stage we'd need to run each pattern through decide() against the effective rules.

That's worth flagging as a real fix for review.ts — filtering candidates down to patterns not already covered by current rules. I also want to check whether review.ts already does this filtering.

Separately, the 147-vs-5 always/once split worries me: the user almost always answers "always," which opencode turns into broad in-memory grants like `herdr *`, `sed *`, `rtk *`, `ssh *` — process-wide permissions this plugin can't revoke. That's a real security observation worth surfacing, and it reinforces why expanding the allowlist for common read-only commands matters: fewer prompts means fewer "always" answers and fewer overly broad grants.

To nail down the actual triggers, I'd want to evaluate each unique pattern against the CLI's check command without the store, but running that for every pattern here might overreach into execution — better to first scope how many unique patterns there are before deciding how deep to go.

1: # Contributing
2: 
3: Thanks for helping to make read-only agents trustworthy. The most useful contributions are **rules**: commands that
4: are safe to run without asking, flags that make a safe command unsafe, and test cases that pin the behaviour down.
5: 
6: ## Setup
7: 
8: ```sh
9: mise install        # bun, node, hk, actionlint, shellcheck, opencode (pinned in mise.toml)
10: mise run setup      # bun install + git hooks
11: mise run check      # what CI runs: lint, format, types, unit tests
12: ```
13: 
14: Without mise you need Bun 1.4+, Node 22+ and `bun install`; `bun run check` does the same as `mise run check`.
15: 
16: ## The shared rules
17: 
18: Everything the plugin decides on its own comes from the JSON files in [`rules/`](rules). They are editor-validated by
19: the JSON Schemas in [`rules/schema/`](rules/schema) and checked by the unit tests.
20: 
21: | File            | Contents                                                                                         |
22: | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
23: | `allow.json`    | opencode bash patterns that read-only agents may run without a prompt. Each has a `reason`.      |
24: | `ask.json`      | patterns that always ask, even when allowed above: flags that write files or run other programs. |
25: | `commands.json` | classification used by the write guard and the learning safety check (see below).                |
26: | `cases.json`    | expected verdicts for commands (`allow` / `ask` / `block`) and for patterns (`ok` true / false). |
27: 
28: Pattern syntax is opencode's: `*` matches anything, `?` one character, and a trailing ` *` also matches the bare
29: command. The **last matching rule wins**, which is why `ask.json` is applied after everything else.
30: 
31: ### Adding a command to the allowlist
32: 
33: An allow rule must be safe in **every** use the pattern can match, not just the common one.
34: 
35: 1. Look for options that write files, delete, or run other programs (`--output`, `-o FILE`, `-exec`, `--pre`, `-x`,
36:    `-i`, `--in-place`, `-delete`, …). If any exists, either do not allow the command, or add the dangerous option to
37:    `ask.json` (a prompt) and, if it is unambiguous, to the analyzer in `src/analyze.ts` (a block).
38: 2. Add the pattern and a short `reason` to `allow.json`. Use `cmd *` for "any arguments", `cmd sub*` for a family of
39:    subcommands, and the exact text for a single use.
40: 3. If the command is reached through the rtk plugin, add the `rtk …` form too.
41: 4. Add cases to `cases.json`: at least one `allow`, plus an `ask` or `block` case for each dangerous option.
42: 5. Run `mise run check`.
43: 
44: Other files:
45: 
46: - **`commands.json` → `hardWrite`:** commands that modify files whatever their arguments. They are blocked.
47: - **`commands.json` → `packageManagers`, `git`:** which subcommands write, and which git subcommands may get a
48:   wildcard rule from `/guard-review`.
49: - **`commands.json` → `herdr`:** `help` (printed help, allowed only as exact commands), `read` (read-only
50:   subcommands, a wildcard may follow), `ui` (what the `herdr-ui` preset in `src/sources.ts` allows inside herdr;
51:   never in `allow.json`) and `write` (blocked). Any other herdr subcommand must be added to `ask.json` as `herdr <sub> *`;
52:   there is no catch-all, because a `herdr *` ask rule would also silence the allowed reads. Keep the four lists
53:   disjoint and `allow.json` in step with `help` and `read` (the unit tests check both).
54: - **`commands.json` → `wildcardSafe`:** commands for which `/guard-review` may offer `cmd *`. Only add a command whose
55:   every read-only use is harmless and whose write options are covered by `ask.json` or the analyzer.
56: 
57: Behaviour that depends on arguments (`tee`, `sed -i`, `find -exec`, `curl -o`, `git branch <name>`, …) lives in
58: `src/analyze.ts`; add a unit test in `test/unit/analyze.test.ts` and a case in `cases.json`.
59: 
60: ## Tests
61: 
62: | Tier        | Command                     | Needs                                    |
63: | ----------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
64: | unit        | `mise run test`             | nothing                                  |
65: | integration | `mise run test:integration` | opencode on `PATH`; builds `dist/` first |
66: | e2e         | `mise run test:e2e`         | opencode credentials; costs a few cents  |
67: 
68: Unit tests include every case in `cases.json`, so a rule change is tested by adding a line there. Integration tests
69: load the built plugin (and a packed tarball) into the real opencode without calling a model. The e2e tests are
70: opt-in because they use a real model.
71: 
72: ## Commits and pull requests
73: 
74: - [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org), enforced by the `commit-msg` hook: `feat(rules): …`,
75:   `fix(analyze): …`, `docs: …`, `test: …`, `build: …`, `ci: …`, `chore: …`.
76: - One logical change per commit. A rule change and its `cases.json` entries go together.
77: - Update `CHANGELOG.md` for user-visible changes.
78: - The pre-commit hook (hk) runs prettier, oxlint, tsc, actionlint and whitespace checks; CI runs the same plus the
79:   tests. Please run `mise run check` before pushing.
80: 
81: ## Reporting a bypass
82: 
83: If a command writes from a read-only agent without being blocked or asked about, open an issue with the command, the
84: agent, and the opencode version. Add it to [`rules/cases.json`](rules/cases.json) as a failing case if you can.
85: 
86: By contributing you agree that your work is released under the [MIT license](LICENSE).

</content>

# Orchestration plan for `opencode-readonly-guard`

## How I'll operate
- **My role:** I run in `wR:p1` and never edit code myself. I scope each work package, start workers, write their briefs, watch them, check their PRs, report to you and keep the roadmap current.
- **Workers:** one opencode agent per work package, named `rog-<topic>`. Each runs in its own git worktree at `[redacted:worktrees_root]/rog-<topic>` on a branch like `feat/<topic>`. Each brief states the goal, the files in scope, the limits, and the bar for done: `mise run check` and `mise run test:integration` both pass, conventional commits, a CHANGELOG entry, and a pushed PR that the worker does not merge.
- **Watching:**
  - I wait on each worker with `herdr agent wait <name> --until done,blocked`.
  - When a worker is blocked on a question or permission prompt, I read its pane and bring the question to you. I never answer permission prompts for you.
- **Review:**
  - You review each PR in the `scm` tab, e.g. `hunk gh pr N`.
  - I check CI with `gh pr checks` and send you a summary of the diff.
  - Nothing merges until you say so.
- **Deploying:** your global opencode config loads the plugin from this checkout's `dist/` (`file://[redacted:repo]`).
  - Running `git pull && mise run build` on `main` therefore updates the plugin for the whole fleet. Each opencode picks it up on restart.
  - Workers build only inside their own worktrees, never in `main`.
- **Cleanup after each merge:** remove the worktree, delete the local and remote branches, and close the worker's tab. Two merged remote branches can be deleted now: `feat/herdr-rules` and `feat/herdr-ui-preset`.

<task id="ses_e62f52903ffeTa4xelPxCnylPV" state="completed">
<task_result>
Summary of herdr v0.9.5 docs on worktrees, plus tab/workspace options and session restore.

**Worktree CLI (cli-reference.mdx, "Worktrees" section)**
- `herdr worktree list [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] [--trust-repository]`
- `herdr worktree create [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] [--branch NAME] [--base REF] [--path PATH] [--label TEXT] [--focus] [--no-focus] [--trust-repository]`
- `herdr worktree open [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] (--path PATH | --branch NAME) [--label TEXT] [--focus] [--no-focus] [--trust-repository]`
- `herdr worktree remove --workspace ID [--force] [--trust-repository]`
- Quote: "Worktrees are normal Herdr workspaces with Git checkout provenance." `create` makes the Git worktree checkout, opens it as a workspace, and "groups it with the parent repo workspace".
- Branch naming: if `--branch` names an existing local branch, Herdr checks it out. Otherwise it creates the branch from `--base`, or from `HEAD` if `--base` is absent.
- Checkout location: without `--path`, the checkout goes under `<worktrees.directory>/<repo>/<branch-slug>`.
- Config key `worktrees.directory`: type string, default `"~/.herdr/worktrees"`. Its description is "Root directory under which Herdr creates <repo>/<branch-slug> checkouts." It is the only worktree location key. Section id is `worktrees`.
- `worktree remove` runs `git worktree remove`, "never deletes the branch", and needs `--force` when Git refuses a dirty checkout.
- `workspace close` "closes only Herdr state" and leaves the checkout on disk. Deleting the checkout requires `worktree remove`.
- Group close: closing a primary workspace while linked-worktree workspaces are open needs `--group`. Without it, the group stays open and the command returns the error `workspace_group_close_required`.
- `tab close`: if `ui.confirm_close` is on and closing the tab would close a whole worktree group, it returns a `confirmation_required` error.
- `--trust-repository`: Git rejects repositories owned by another user by default. The flag trusts the resolved path "for that command only", and Herdr does not change your Git config.
- Remote use: `herdr --machine "Build machine" worktree create --cwd /srv/project --branch review`. Remote worktree paths must be absolute, `~`, or start with `~/`, and are expanded on the server.
- Plugins: the plugin example `ogulcancelik/herdr-plugin-examples/worktree-bootstrap` is mentioned as an install example.

**Worktree keybindings and sidebar (config-reference.json)**
- `keys.new_worktree` defaults to `"prefix+shift+g"` ("Create a Git worktree from the selected workspace").
- `keys.open_worktree` is unset by default.
- `keys.remove_worktree` is unset by default. Description: "Delete the selected managed worktree checkout after confirmation."
- `ui.sidebar.spaces.row_gap` defaults to `0`. It sets "Blank terminal rows between worktree groups and unrelated top-level Spaces. Worktree parents and their indented children remain packed."
- So linked worktrees appear in the sidebar's Space list as indented children under their parent repo workspace.
- `ui.sidebar.spaces.rows` defaults to `[["state_icon", "workspace"], ["branch", "git_status"]]`, which shows the branch and git status per Space.
- `ui.confirm_close` defaults to `true`.

**`herdr workspace create`**
- `herdr workspace create [--cwd PATH] [--label TEXT] [--env KEY=VALUE] [--focus] [--no-focus]`
- It also creates the first tab and root pane. The response has `.result.workspace.workspace_id`, `.result.tab.tab_id` and `.result.root_pane.pane_id`.
- Related commands: `workspace list|get|focus|rename|report-metadata`, and `workspace close <id> [--group]`.

**`herdr tab create`**
- `herdr tab create [--workspace <workspace_id>] [--cwd PATH] [--label TEXT] [--env KEY=VALUE] [--focus] [--no-focus]`
- Without `--workspace` it uses the active workspace and fails if none exists.
- The response has `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`.
- Focus is unchanged by default. `--focus` selects the new layout, and `--no-focus` states the default explicitly.
- Without `--cwd`, the `terminal.new_cwd` policy applies: values `follow` (default), `home`, `current`, `path`.
- Each `--env` adds or replaces a variable in the new root shell. It can be repeated.
- The `ui.prompt_new_tab_name` default is `true`. It applies only to the TUI.

**Session restore (session-state.mdx)**
- Yes, opencode agents are resumed after a server restart, subject to conditions below.
- Native agent session restore is on by default. Setting `[session] resume_agents_on_restore = false` disables it.
- OpenCode needs integration version `5` or newer. The resume command is `opencode --session <id>`. Run `herdr integration install opencode` and `herdr integration status` to check.
- Only panes that reported a native session reference through an official integration, or whose agent reported its own resume command, are resumed.
- Unsupported, missing, invalid, duplicated or stale references restore as plain shells in the saved cwd.
- Resume happens after a client attaches and provides terminal size and theme. Eligible panes across all workspaces and tabs resume without needing focus.
- `session.startup_per_agent_delay_ms` defaults to `100`. It spaces automatic restores, and the first agent starts without the delay.
- Server restart does not keep processes running. It restores workspaces, tabs, panes, cwd, layout and focus. Recent screen content returns only if `[experimental] pane_history = true`, which is off by default.
- Detach and reattach keeps everything running.
- Resume commands run only for `agent start` kinds or hooks that report them. `pane report-agent` takes `-- RESUME_COMMAND...`. The first argument must be a plain command on `PATH`, and no argument may contain an apostrophe.

**Not stated in the docs**
- concepts.mdx and agent-automation.mdx say nothing about worktrees, workspace groups or `--group`.
- No exact slug rules for `<branch-slug>`, for example how `/` in `feature/x` is handled.
- No default branch name when `--branch` is omitted, and no default `--label`.
- No JSON response schema for `worktree create|open|list|remove`. The doc doesn't say whether `.result.workspace` or `.result.root_pane` appear, or what `list` returns.
- No statement on what `worktree remove` does to the workspace entry beyond running `git worktree remove`. It does not say if the Herdr workspace closes, or what happens to other linked workspaces.
- No statement on whether `worktree remove` works on the primary workspace's checkout.
- No statement on how a group is persisted across restart, or whether worktrees are listed in `workspace list` with a parent or group field.
- No detail on what `worktree open` does when the checkout is already open, or whether `--branch` there needs the branch to be checked out in an existing worktree.
- No mention of a worktree-specific `workspace create` option.
- `worktrees.directory` is the only location key found, and there are no per-repo overrides.
</task_result>

The plan is final. On the open question about the orchestrator role and a possible rename:

## Multiclass support, rename and scope
You're right that it's a vision question.
- **Keep the name.** If you frame an orchestrator as "read-only for code, plus control-plane capabilities", it's still a guard against writes. The `herdr-ui` preset already took a small step that way.
- **Rename.** If the direction is several roles (orchestrator, reviewer, tester, release…), each with its own capabilities, the project becomes a role-based shell policy engine. Then "readonly" is misleading.
- **Timing matters more than the choice:** renaming is cheap now and expensive after the npm publish in step 5. A rename touches:
  - the package, CLI, repo and `/guard-review` names
  - the `readonly-guard.json` store files and the `READONLY_GUARD_*` environment variables
  - the `file:///…` path in your global config
  - the `rog-` alias itself

My recommendation is to settle it in step 4 rather than add a feature step now. Steps 1 to 3 hardly depend on the name. In the meantime I run in build mode and edit no code by choice.

| 4 | Vision and scope (orchestrator class, multiclass, rename) plus TODO triage | me drafts, you decide | must come before 5 |

**Topology**
- One herdr worktree workspace per workstream, grouped under `wR` and checked out at `[redacted:worktrees_root]/rog-<topic>`.
- Workers on the same worktree each get a tab in that workspace. A worktree is a workstream, so successive branches such as PR 1.1, then 1.2, then 1.3 reuse it.
- Each workspace also gets a review tab where I open hunk once CI passes.

**Review loop**
1. The worker opens a PR.
2. I watch CI. If it fails, I send the worker the failure log, up to 3 times before coming to you.
3. When CI passes, I open hunk in the review tab and notify you.
4. You give the go, then I merge.
5. I run `git pull && mise run build` in `main` to update the fleet's plugin, and tell you which agents to restart.
6. I remove the worktree and delete the local branch. Remote branches are kept.

5. Watch both and relay any prompt to you.

Expect a small conflict: both PRs edit `CHANGELOG.md`, so whichever merges second rebases.

Usage: herdr agent prompt <TARGET> <TEXT> [OPTIONS]

      --wait

  - **Renovate dry run:** the worker ran it locally against GitHub with your `gh` token, in read-only mode.
  - **Renovate PRs:** it would open five PRs, including `node.js to v26` and `opencode to v1.19.5`.
    - **node 26:** you'll probably want to cap `node` at 24; I can have the worker add that before merge.
    - **opencode 1.19.5:** it is capped below 2.0. Bumping it needs a `test:integration` run.
  - **Action pinning:** your workflows use tags, not SHAs. Renovate's first Actions PR will pin them.
  - **Manual step:** you have to install the Renovate GitHub app on the repo.

**`rog-rules`**
- It accepted my guidance and is now on commits 1 to 3: the `git remote -v add` analyzer bypass fix, the sole `--help` fix, and the help rules layer.
- It found a real bug: `git remote -v add x url` slips past the write guard today.
- No PR yet.

**Two housekeeping notes**
- git hooks are not installed in this repo (`.git/hooks` has only samples), so commit-message and pre-commit checks don't run locally. Workers follow the conventions by hand and CI is the safety net.
- Merging #3 won't touch the fleet's plugin: it contains no `src/` changes. I'll only pull and rebuild `main` after PR 1.1.

| sort, uniq, cut, tr, comm, join, diff, column | 88 | 1 |
| basename, dirname, strings | 6 | 0 |
| date, du, df, pgrep | 32 | 1 |
| whoami, id, hostname, getent, env, command -v | 18 | 0 |
| git branch, tag, remote, config, ls-tree, rev-list, merge-base, ls-remote, worktree | 29 | 3 |

| npm view | 10 | 0 |

| env-var prefix (PR 1.3) | 28 | 30 |
| sysadmin reads (PR 1.2): pacman, flatpak, snap, docker, podman, virsh, VBoxManage, vagrant, ip, findmnt, lsblk, systemctl, … | 35 | 38 |
| other (tool `--version`, git grep / check-ignore / for-each-ref, gh, insync, scripts, …) | 66 | 67 |
| **total stages asking** | **680** | **274** |

Prompts with at least one stage still asking: 146 → 106.

The "kept on purpose", prefix and sysadmin rows grow a little because `decide()` reports the first stage that asks. Once `echo` no longer asks, a later `sed` in the same stage becomes visible.

The few targeted commands left all ask on purpose:
- `git config --global user.name`, `git config core.hooksPath`: `git config KEY` alone stays a prompt, as decided.
- `df --output=avail`: matches the generic `* --output*` rule.
- One `echo` and one `grep` whose text contains `--delete-excluded`: they match the generic `*-delete*` find rule.

## What changes

**Write guard (`src/analyze.ts`).** Each change was written as a failing test first.
- `git remote -v add|rename|remove|set-url …` was not blocked: only the first argument was compared. Now only listing, `show` and `get-url` pass.
- A sole trailing `--help` after a git, herdr, npm or mise subcommand path is not that subcommand's write (`herdr worktree create --help`, `npm install --help`). `-h` and `--help` next to other arguments are judged as before.
- git branch and tag, checked against git 2.53:
  - `-v`, `-vv`, `--verbose`, `--sort`, `--format` and `--color` do not switch to list mode, so `git branch -v NAME` and `git tag --sort=x NAME` create a ref. The guard used to let them through; it now blocks them.
  - Write options are also caught when abbreviated (`git branch -a --edit-desc` edits the description) and in bundles (`-rd`).
  - `git tag -n1 NAME`, which only lists, is no longer blocked.
- `git ls-remote --upload-pack/--exec=CMD` is blocked when CMD writes.
- `sort`:
  - `--o`/`--out` abbreviations of `--output` are blocked like `-o`.
  - `--compress-program=PROG` is blocked when PROG writes (compressors pass).
- `uniq`: the OUTPUT operand is now parsed correctly. `uniq - out`, `uniq in 5` and `uniq -- -x out` were missed; `-` or the null device as OUTPUT is fine.
- `date -s/--set` (any abbreviation) and a `MMDDhhmm` operand are blocked. Option values are parsed, so `date -d tomorrow` passes.
- `hostname NAME`, `-F/--file` and `-b` are blocked.
- `set` is added to the package-manager write subcommands: `mise set K=V` writes mise.toml, and `npm set` and `yarn set` write their configuration.

**Allowlist (`rules/allow.json`) and always-ask flags (`rules/ask.json`).**
- Allowed with any arguments: echo, printf, cut, tr, sort, uniq, comm, join, diff, basename, dirname, strings, date, du, df, pgrep, whoami, id, getent, printenv, `command -v|-V`.
- Allowed as exact commands only: `env` (`env CMD` runs CMD) and the printing forms of hostname.
- git reads:
  - with any arguments: `ls-tree`, `rev-list`, `merge-base`, `worktree list`, `ls-remote`;
  - remote: the bare command, `-v`, `show` and `get-url`;
  - branch: the bare command, `--show-current`, the exact `-v`/`-vv`, and the list-mode flags followed by anything (`-a`, `-r`, `-l`, `--list`, `--contains`, `--merged`, `--points-at`, …);
  - tag: the bare command and `-l`, `--list`, `-n<N>`, `--contains`, …;
  - config: `--get*`, `--list*`, `-l`, `get` and `list`, also after `--global` or `--local`.

{
  "filePath": "/tmp/opencode/bin/watch",
  "content": "#!/usr/bin/env bash\n# watch NAME...: poll workers; answer \"Allow once\" (never \"always\") to a blocked worker only when the prompt is a\n# single-line shell command that the shared read-only rules allow (node dist/cli.js check --no-store exits 0).\n# Returns (exit 0) as soon as a worker is idle/done, or when a blocked prompt is NOT auto-answerable (printed).\n# Usage: watch [--max SECONDS] NAME...\nset -u\nCLI=[redacted:repo]:dist/cli.js\nLOG=/tmp/opencode/answers.log\nmax=1500\nif [ \"${1:-}\" = --max ]; then max=$2; shift 2; fi\nnames=(\"$@\")\nstart=$SECONDS\nwhile [ $((SECONDS - start)) -lt \"$max\" ]; do\n  for name in \"${names[@]}\"; do\n    status=$(herdr agent get \"$name\" 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.result.agent.agent_status // \"gone\"')\n    case $status in\n      idle | done | gone | unknown)\n        echo \"$name: $status\"\n        exit 0\n        ;;\n      blocked)\n        screen=$(herdr agent read \"$name\" --source visible --lines 40 2>&1 | sed 's/[[:space:]]*[█▄▀]*$//')\n        block=$(printf '%s\\n' \"$screen\" | sed -n '/Permission required/,/Allow once/p')\n        if printf '%s\\n' \"$block\" | grep -q '# Shell command'; then\n          body=$(printf '%s\\n' \"$block\" | sed -n '/# Shell command/,/Allow once/p' | sed '1d;$d' | sed 's/^[[:space:]]*┃[[:space:]]\\{0,2\\}//' | grep -v '^\\s*$')\n          if [ \"$(printf '%s\\n' \"$body\" | wc -l)\" -eq 1 ] && [[ $body == '$ '* ]]; then\n            cmd=${body#\\$ }\n            if node \"$CLI\" check --no-store \"$cmd\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n              herdr agent send-keys \"$name\" enter >/dev/null 2>&1\n              printf '%s %s ALLOW-ONCE %s\\n' \"$(date +%T)\" \"$name\" \"$cmd\" >>\"$LOG\"\n              sleep 4\n              continue\n            fi\n          fi\n        fi\n        echo \"$name: blocked, needs the coordinator or the maintainer\"\n        printf '%s\\n' \"$block\"\n        exit 0\n        ;;\n    esac\n  done\n  sleep 8\ndone\necho \"watch: timeout after ${max}s\"\n"
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: box.sh <name> <project-plugin-json> [global-plugin-json]  -> creates /tmp/opencode/exp/<name>
set -euo pipefail
name=$1; project_plugins=$2; global_plugins=${3:-}
dir=/tmp/opencode/exp/$name
rm -rf "$dir"
mkdir -p "$dir/project" "$dir/xdg/config/opencode" "$dir/xdg/data" "$dir/xdg/cache" "$dir/xdg/state"
git -C "$dir/project" init -q
git -C "$dir/project" -c user.name=t -c user.email=t@e commit -q --allow-empty -m init
printf '{ "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "plugin": %s }\n' "$project_plugins" > "$dir/project/opencode.json"
if [ -n "$global_plugins" ]; then
  printf '{ "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "plugin": %s }\n' "$global_plugins" > "$dir/xdg/config/opencode/opencode.json"
fi
cat > "$dir/env.sh" <<EOF
for v in \$(env | grep -o '^HERDR_[A-Z_]*'); do unset \$v; done
export XDG_CONFIG_HOME=$dir/xdg/config XDG_DATA_HOME=$dir/xdg/data XDG_CACHE_HOME=$dir/xdg/cache XDG_STATE_HOME=$dir/xdg/state
export READONLY_GUARD_STORE=$dir/store.json READONLY_GUARD_DATA=$dir/log PWD=$dir/project
cd $dir/project
EOF
echo "$dir"

     source, and ran sandboxed probes in /tmp/opencode/exp.
     How opencode loads plugins
     - Plugins load once per opencode instance, i.e. per directory (serve can hold several). All plugins of an instance get the same PluginInput object.
     - Every server() runs first, global entries before project ones. Then every config hook runs, in the same order.
     - opencode itself dedupes plugin entries: the same file:// spec, or the same npm name, keeps only the last one. Different specs are not deduped, so you
       get 2 copies.
     - A probe confirmed it: two copies of the plugin see the same input object.
     - Import fails (no dist/, no node_modules): opencode only publishes a session.error event. That shows as a TUI toast only if a TUI is already listening.
       Nothing is logged at any level, and debug config exits 0 and still lists the spec.
     - server() throws (corrupt rules/allow.json): one ERROR line, "failed to load plugin", in opencode's log, and the plugin is dropped.
     1. Single load (new src/instances.ts)
     - A registry on globalThis[Symbol.for("opencode-readonly-guard/instances@1")], a WeakMap keyed by the PluginInput object. It is shared across module
       copies but kept per opencode instance; a plain process-wide flag would break servers that hold several directories.
     - A copy registers after its setup succeeds. The last one registered wins, which is the project entry, and its options replace the global ones entirely (
       opencode's own dedupe works the same way).
     - In the losing copy:
       - the config hook returns without touching the config;
       - tool.execute.before, event and chat.params do nothing;
       - its tools are still registered (it can't know at server() time that it will lose), so their execute hands over to the winner. Its own read-only
         agent list stays empty.
     - At runtime the winner is the last copy that actually injected rules, so a copy without rules is never in charge.
     - Option warnings move into the config hook. The init event gains copies and module (the file that is active).
     2. Dependency: bundle it. The build becomes tsc --emitDeclarationOnly plus bun build src/index.ts src/cli.ts --target node.
     - This puts zod and the tool() helper inside the built file: dist/index.js is 457 KB, cli.js 57 KB. rules/ is still read from ../rules.
     - Tested: opencode loads it from a directory without node_modules, and the tool arguments still work as before (limit stays optional and keeps its
       description).
     - Rejected alternatives: opencode's "legacy" JSON-schema arguments (every argument becomes required and nothing is validated), and a lazy import (loses
       the tools when the dependency is missing).
     3. Load failures. A plugin that fails to import cannot report anything itself; I'll say so in the README.
     - (a) In the plugin: if setup fails (the rules files), write an error event (where: "load") and fail closed. Read-only agents then get *: ask (their own
       deny rules are kept) and one toast. This only applies when no working copy is loaded.
     - (b) CLI doctor: runs opencode debug config in the current directory and reports:
       - which configured copies are this plugin, and which one wins;
       - which agents carry the plugin's rules (they have readonly_guard_review: deny), with rule counts;
       - for each file:// copy, whether its entry imports in a child process, with the reason if not (e.g. "dist missing, run mise run build");
       - the last init or error event from the log.
       - It exits 1 when the guard is not active. Code goes in a new src/doctor.ts; commands.ts only gets the help line, a case, and a CliIo.capture method.
     4. Tests (failing first)
     - Unit:
       - two server() calls on one input: one injection using the second copy's options, one call event, tools hand over to the winner;
       - a failed setup fails closed;
       - doctor with a fake capture.
     - Integration (sandbox() gains a globalPlugin option):
       - a packed tarball extracted without node_modules: plan gets the rules, and dist/ has no bare imports;
       - a global copy plus a project entry with options: one init per run, copies: 2, the project's allow and exclude: explore apply;
       - doctor reports active, and exits 1 with the reason for a copy without dist/.
     5. Dogfooding: "plugin": ["."] in the repo's opencode.json. opencode resolves it against that file's directory, so it works in every clone and worktree.
     - Main checkout: same spec as your global entry, so opencode dedupes it.
     - A worktree: its own build wins over the global copy.
     - No build: silently skipped, and the global copy (if any) keeps guarding.

     Risks
     - The dedupe relies on opencode passing one input object per instance. If that changes, we fall back to today's double load, never to no guard, and the
       integration test catches it when opencode is bumped.
     - Project options replace global ones. A repo's config can already rewrite permissions or load its own plugins, so this adds no new exposure.

_Thinking:_
I'm thinking through the stash-and-build sequence in the test — stashing worktree changes, rebuilding, running the CLI command, then popping the stash back. This checks whether the previous build state behaves correctly before the new changes are reapplied.

The real risk is that `git stash` operates on a repository-wide stash stack shared across worktrees, so if another worktree stashes something during this window, the pop could restore the wrong changes. It's unlikely in a short timeframe, and since this touches only the worker's own working tree, I'll allow it despite the small residual risk — this falls slightly outside my usual approval criteria but seems reasonable as a one-off. The earlier mismatch on the `check --no-store` test was just due to broken quoting in my own test command, not a real issue.


_Thinking:_
Using `git stash -q`, rebuilding, then `git stash pop -q` temporarily shelves the worker's changes to compare against the previous build; since the stash list is shared across worktrees, there's a slim chance a `pop` grabs another worktree's stash. Given the short window and `rog-rules` stashing only rarely, I'll accept that risk and answer "once".

Second of three PRs that update the allowlist from what read-only agents ran in real sessions (PR #4 was the first). This one covers the sysadmin reads: systemd, disks and network, packages, containers and VMs. It also adds the git reads and exact `--version` commands parked in #4, `mise version|which|where`, and fixes two false blocks (bare `mount`, `systemctl show-environment`).

## Before / after

Same method as #4. Every unique `.patterns[]` entry of the logged `asked` bash events goes through `decide()` with the shared rules only, comparing `main` (f8de2bd) with this branch. The log has grown since #4: 156 prompts, 862 unique stages. The counts are stages that still ask.

| Commands | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| systemctl, journalctl | 5 | 0 |
| lsblk, findmnt, mount, ip | 4 | 0 |
| pacman, flatpak, snap | 10 | 0 |
| docker, podman | 3 | 0 |
| virsh, VBoxManage, vagrant | 8 | 0 |
| git grep, check-ignore, show-ref, for-each-ref, hash-object | 7 | 0 |
| exact `--version` (node, python3, bun, npm, git, gh, opencode, hk, chezmoi, …), `mise version\|which\|where` | 8 | 0 |
| kept on purpose: sed, awk, python3, node, sqlite3, ssh, rtk ssh, rtk proxy, xargs | 117 | 115 |
| kept on purpose: `git -C`, `rtk git -C`, `git config KEY` | 31 | 31 |
| env-var prefix and bare statements (PR 1.3) | 35 | 35 |
| other (insync, gh, ssh-keygen, sha256sum, `/usr/bin/ls`, scripts, tools not in scope, …) | 69 | 68 |
| **total stages asking** | **297** | **249** |

Prompts with at least one stage still asking: 115 → 102. Every sysadmin command in the log is now allowed. The 2 fewer in "kept on purpose" are the exact `node --version` and `python3 --version`.

## What changes

All the new argument parsers live in a new module, `src/programs.ts`. Each one follows the program's own option rules: abbreviations, bundled short options, and which options take a value. Every analyzer change was written as a failing test first, and where possible the behaviour was checked against the real program.

**systemd**
- Allowed: `systemctl [--user] <verb> *` for the read verbs (status, show, cat, is-active|enabled|failed|system-running, list-units|unit-files|timers|sockets|dependencies|jobs, show-environment, get-default); `rtk systemctl status *`; `journalctl *`.
- Ask:
  - `systemctl -H/--host` (another host over ssh) and `-M/--machine` (a container).
  - journalctl's maintenance and write options (`--vacuum-*`, `--rotate`, `--flush`, `--sync`, `--synchronize-on-exit`, `--relinquish-var`, `--smart-relinquish-var`, `--setup-keys`, `--update-catalog`, `--cursor-file`), each from its shortest prefix.
- Guard:
  - blocks `-H`/`-M` in a bundle (`status -aH host`) or abbreviated (`--ho=host`), because the ask rules cannot see them there: "write -H HOST as a separate option so it asks".
  - finds the verb after options that take a value, so `systemctl -t service list-units` is no longer blocked;
  - treats show-environment and get-default as reads;
  - blocks journalctl's maintenance options in any getopt abbreviation (`--rot` and `--vac=1d` used to pass).

**Disks and network**
- Allowed: `lsblk *`, `findmnt *`, and the exact `mount` and `mount -l`.
- ip: `ip a|addr|address|l|link|r|ro|route|n|neigh|neighbor|neighbour *` and `ip -br|-4|-6|-j <object> *` (32 rules).
- Guard:
  - mount: only `mount`, `mount -l` and `mount [-l] -t TYPE` pass; every other mount stays blocked.
  - ip follows the iproute2 sources: `matches()` prefixes, resolved in the order of each object's verb table, so `ip link s` is set and `ip a s` is show.
  - It blocks add, change, replace, delete, set, flush, prepend, append, test, restore and property in any abbreviation, also after the global options (including `-color=always`).

Now shifting to the actual question: should the watch helper be added to this project? My instinct is no — the repo is scoped as a plugin restricting read-only agents, whereas the watch helper is really an orchestration tool for coordinating worker agents, which falls outside what the README and AGENTS scope define, especially while the broader orchestrator/multiclass question is still unresolved.

On top of the scope mismatch, there's a quality problem: it's hard-coded to this specific machine's paths, relies on opencode's undocumented sqlite schema, and does fragile screen-scraping of the TUI for permission prompts — none of it versioned, tested, or resilient to UI changes. And safety-wise, auto-approving permission prompts is delicate territory; I noticed the DB-vs-screen comparison only checks the first 60 characters against the screen text, which could leave room for subtle holes like path traversal slipping through unnoticed.

Really, most of these ~45 approval prompts are a symptom of an overly restrictive opencode.json requiring "ask" on everything — the cleaner fix is to widen the allowlist for reads, or implement the plugin's TODO to have `permission.hook("evaluate")` answer prompts directly using the analyzer's verdict instead of screen-scraping at all. What's worth salvaging from this experiment is the core idea and a couple of pieces, like the quote-aware command splitter — though that duplicates functionality the plugin's shell tokenizer already provides, so it'd be better to reuse that directly.

As for where this helper script belongs: I don't think it should live in this repo. If I keep it, it probably fits better as fleet/orchestration tooling — maybe a dotfiles repo, the multi-repo orchestration study, or as a documented skill under the agents skills directory, rather than becoming part of this project's scope.

No, not as it stands. Keep it out of this repo, and fix the cause of the prompts instead.

**Why not**
- **Scope:** the repo is a plugin that restricts read-only agents. The helper drives worker agents under herdr, which is orchestration. Putting it here would settle the step-4 question (orchestrator role, scope, rename) before you've decided it.
- **Fragility:** it only works on this machine.
  - **Hard-coded paths:** it names `~/...` and `/tmp/opencode`.
  - **Undocumented internals:** it reads opencode's SQLite `part` table and scrapes the TUI text "Permission required / Allow once".
  - **Ad hoc patterns:** the dev-loop regexes were added one prompt at a time, and nothing tests them.
- **Risk:** auto-pressing Enter on permission prompts is a safety tool. A bug there means a write gets approved, so it deserves proper tests, and a screen scraper doesn't give you that.
- **Wrong layer:** about 45 prompts came up, nearly all reads that the project `opencode.json` (`* ask`, short allow list) doesn't cover. The prompt traffic is a symptom of that.

**What I'd do instead**
1. **Widen `opencode.json` for reads.** The shared patterns in `rules/allow.json` already use opencode's syntax. A small PR could reuse them for the repo's agents, or generate the bash allow list from `bun src/cli.ts rules --json`. That's versioned and reviewed.
2. **Let the plugin do it.** The opencode 2.x `permission.hook("evaluate")` is already in TODO as "answering prompts with the analyzer's verdict".
3. **If you still want the helper,** put it with your fleet tooling (chezmoi or an agent skill). After PRs 1.3 and 1.4 it shrinks to about 30 lines. Most of the length is workarounds for allowlist gaps (`fold`, bare `B=...;`), and `stages.mjs` duplicates `src/shell.ts`.

Say if you want option 1 as a PR for `rog-setup`, or a TODO line.

- **Timing:** `.git/config` was modified at 20:05:43, five seconds after `rog-setup`'s commit 9e98138 at 20:05:38, followed by its push.

- **Pattern:** every time, it pointed at the worktree that had just committed or pushed.
- **Risk while it's set:** `git` in `main` operates on that worker's files, so a commit in `main` could include them.
- **Not yet proven:** this is a hypothesis, and a reproduction in a scratch repo would confirm it.

404:Tokens render in their configured order. Herdr normally separates adjacent values with ` · ` and uses a single space after `state_icon`. Missing values and their separators disappear; a row disappears when none of its tokens have a value. Existing custom rows remain unchanged, so add `machine` explicitly if you want machine identity in a custom multi-machine layout. Each layout may contain at most 16 rows, with at most 16 tokens in each row.

406-A token entry can also be an inline style table:

413-]

415-
416-`fg` accepts strict `#RGB` or `#RRGGBB`. `bold` and `dim` accept booleans. Omitted fields preserve the token's contextual style; explicit `false` removes that modifier. Styling applies to one occurrence, so the same token may look different in another row or agent override. A foreground override replaces all semantic foregrounds inside that occurrence: for example, styled `git_status` ahead and behind counts use one color instead of their default green and red. Token styles never change separators or row backgrounds.
417-
418:Text-valued tokens also accept up to 16 ordered `rules`. Each rule contains exactly one condition—`equals`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `gt`, or `lt`—and optional `fg`, `bold`, and `dim` overrides:
419-
420-```toml

422-rows = [
423-  ["state_icon", "workspace", "tab"],
424-  [{ token = "machine", fg = "#fff", rules = [{ equals = "Local", fg = "#f55" }, { equals = "Fedora", ignore_case = true, fg = "#51a2da" }] }, "agent"],
425-  [{ token = "$load", fg = "#fff", rules = [{ gt = 80, fg = "#f55", bold = true }, { gt = 50, fg = "#fc0" }] }],
426-]
427-```
428-
429:The first matching rule wins. Its specified style fields override the occurrence's defaults; unspecified fields inherit them. If no rule matches, the defaults remain. Matching uses the full token value before display truncation. Set `hide = true` on a rule to remove the matching token and its separator; rows with no remaining tokens also disappear. For example, `{ token = "machine", fg = "#61afef", rules = [{ equals = "Local", hide = true }] }` hides the machine token when its label is exactly `Local`. This compares the label, not the connection type. With `hide = false` or omitted, the token stays visible. A rule with no overrides still stops matching and keeps the defaults.
430-
431-`equals`, `contains`, and `starts_with` take strings and are case-sensitive. Add `ignore_case = true` for ASCII case-insensitive matching; non-ASCII characters remain case-sensitive. Empty strings follow ordinary string matching: empty `equals` matches only an empty value, while empty `contains` or `starts_with` matches any present value.
432-
433-`gt` and `lt` take finite numeric thresholds and compare strictly greater or less, not equal. Values must parse completely as finite numbers; decimal and exponent forms work, but whitespace, units, `NaN`, and infinity do not match. `ignore_case` is not accepted on numeric rules. Comparisons use floating-point numbers, not exact large-integer arithmetic.
434-
435:Rules work with text-valued built-ins and custom `$name` tokens in Agent rows, `rows_by_agent` overrides, and Space rows. Custom tokens match their reported value: `$load` reporting `"90"` selects red and bold above, `"60"` selects yellow, and `"90%"` keeps white. Unreported tokens still disappear. `state_icon` and composite `git_status` accept fixed styles only, not rules. Unknown conditions and malformed rules are rejected when loading config; regex, fuzzy matching, and scripts are not supported.

Correct way to use hk with parallel agents with worktrees?
Suppose several coding agents work in worktrees at the same time, each might have subagents working and committing on their own pace, with `hk` as the pre-commit hook. What is the intended configuration for this setup?

I have custom scripts for the flow:
- PostToolUse runs read-only, non-formatting linters for coding agents on touched files to feedback immediately
- formatters run in a git pre-commit hook to the index (`git cat-file blob`) directly

It works okay, but has some performance issues. Instead of optimizing its performance, I'm looking into `hk` to replace the setup, but got some issues.

The [guide on stashing](https://hk.jdx.dev/hooks.html#stashing-and-partial-commits) recommends `stash = "git"` whenever the staged version must be isolated, but it has bugs if multiple agents are running at the same time. If turning it off `stash = "none"`, it still doesn't fit well for multiple agents:

1. `stash = "git"` keeps partially staged files intact, but puts hk's entry on the `refs/stash` that every worktree shares. Stash commands in other worktrees may operate on that entry at the same time. Also, though the lock that protects the entry from other hk processes makes hooks in

hk 2.8.1 stops pre-commit hooks in different linked worktrees from taking each other's stash entries, and lets those hooks run in parallel. It also removes a deprecation warning printed by the `ryl_markdown` builtin.

## Fixed

- **Stashing is now separate for each linked worktree** ([#1747](https://github.com/jdx/hk/pull/1747), @jdx). With `stash = "git"`, hk used to put its entry on `refs/stash`, and every linked worktree shares that stack. A `git stash pop`, `drop` or `push` in one worktree could take hk's entry while a hook was running in another worktree. The hook then failed with "hk's stash entry … is no longer in the stash list", and its unstaged and untracked changes were left in a stash that the other worktree could pop. hk now keeps its entry under a private ref, `refs/hk/stash/<commit-id>`, which `git stash` never reads or writes. `hk-stash.lock` now lives in each worktree's own git directory, so hooks in different worktrees run in parallel. Two hk processes in the same worktree still take turns. Entries that older hk versions pushed onto `git stash` can still be restored or dropped. Fixes [#1746](https://github.com/jdx/hk/issues/1746).

  `git stash list` no longer shows hk's entries. To inspect or recover one, use its commit id:

  ```bash
  git for-each-ref refs/hk/stash
  git stash show -p <commit-id>
  git stash apply <commit-id>
  git update-ref -d refs/hk/stash/<commit-id>
  ```

- **`ryl_markdown` no longer prints a deprecation warning** ([#1741](https://github.com/jdx/hk/pull/1741), @illesnagy1). The builtin ran bare `ryl --markdown <paths>`, which made ryl print `bare ryl <paths> is deprecated`. Like the `ryl` builtin, it now runs `ryl check`.
- **Nushell completions no longer print a deprecation warning on nushell 0.116** ([#1749](https://github.com/jdx/hk/pull/1749)). This comes from updating usage-rs to 7.1.1, which fixes the completer generated by `hk completion nu`.

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/jdx/hk/compare/v2.8.0...v2.8.1


## 💚 Sponsor hk

hk is built and maintained by [@jdx](https://github.com/jdx), an open source developer at [**entire.io**](https://entire.io/), the title sponsor of his open source work.

If hk speeds up your pre-commit loop or makes linting less painful, please consider becoming an [individual or company sponsor](https://jdx.dev/sponsors.html). Your support funds ongoing development and helps keep hk fast, free, and independent.


```

## Widening `opencode.json`: you're right, I won't do it
The project's guarantees for an allowed pattern rely on two things together: the `ask.json` flags evaluated after the allowlist, and the write guard (`tool.execute.before`). Both apply only to read-only agents.

If I copied `rules/allow.json` into `opencode.json` for build workers, `find *`, `sort *` and `git branch*` would run unguarded, so `find / -delete` could run with no prompt at all. That defeats the purpose.

What the workers need instead is a role in the plugin:
- reads go through the shared allowlist, the ask flags and the write guard;
- writes are allowed only in the worker's own worktree and in scratch directories;
- git can push its own branch, but never merges.

That's the "role-based permissions" direction you mentioned. My delegation rules, the watcher (which already uses the plugin's own `check` as its oracle) and `answers.log` (about 50 decisions, each with a reason) together form the specification and the test data for that role. They belong in step 4. Until then, I keep answering prompts with the watcher.

## The name in the agents panel
- **What the panel shows:** the default layout is two lines.
  - Line 1 is the workspace and tab (`opencode-readonly-guard · orch`).
  - Line 2 is the detected agent kind (`opencode`).
  - The herdr agent name `rog-orch` exists in the API, but the panel has no token for it.
- **What I'd run:** `herdr pane report-metadata wR:p1 --source rog:orch --agent opencode --display-agent rog-orch` turns line 2 into `rog-orch`.
  - The `--agent opencode` guard limits it to while opencode occupies the pane.
  - I'd do the same for every `rog-*` worker when I start it.
  - A herdr server restart drops it, so I'd re-apply it then.
- **Optional:** putting the name on line 1 would mean changing `ui.sidebar.agents.rows` in your herdr config. That lives in your dotfiles, not this repo.

## A new blocker: hk 2.8.0 and linked worktrees
- The repo pins hk 2.8.0, and `hk.pkl` uses `stash = "git"` for pre-commit.
- hk 2.8.1 fixed "Stashing is now separate for each linked worktree" (jdx/hk#1746, #1747). In 2.8.0, hk's stash entry sits on the shared `refs/stash`, so a hook in one worktree can take another worktree's entry. That can lose a worker's unstaged changes.
- With four workers committing in parallel, that is a real risk. It may also be related to the `core.worktree` writes; the reproduction will tell.
- **Fix:** bump hk to 2.11.0 (the latest) in `mise.toml` and in the two `hk.pkl` package URLs, before starting the four workers.
